lessons.title: Building an AI Script
lessons.content_md:
# The Capstone Project 🏆

You've learned how AI works. Now it's time to actually use it. We are going to write a Python script that calls a real AI API (like Google Gemini or OpenAI) and push the code to GitHub.

## Step 1: Get Your API Key

First, you need an **API Key**. This is a secret password that allows your code to talk to the AI provider's servers. Go to the provider's developer console and generate a free API key.

<flipcard front="🔑 What is an API Key?" back="A unique string of characters used to authenticate your script so the AI provider knows who is making the request."></flipcard>

## Step 2: Write the Python Code

Create a new file called `ai_assistant.py` and install the provider's Python library (e.g., `pip install google-genai`).

Write a simple script that asks the AI a question:

```python
import os
from google import genai

client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ.get("GEMINI_API_KEY"))

response = client.models.generate_content(
    model='gemini-2.5-flash',
    contents='Explain Quantum Computing to a 5 year old.',
)

print(response.text)
```

## Step 3: Secure Your Key

**NEVER** paste your API key directly into your code if you are going to put it on the internet. Hackers will steal it. Instead, save it as an Environment Variable on your computer.

<flipcard front="🛑 What happens if I put my API Key on GitHub?" back="Bots constantly scan GitHub for exposed keys. They will steal yours and run up thousands of dollars in server charges on your account!"></flipcard>

## Step 4: Push to GitHub

Initialize a git repository, commit your code, and push it to your GitHub profile to show the world what you've built!

<flipcard front="➡️ What's next?" back="This script is your warm-up. In the next two lessons you'll plan a full capstone and submit it to the AI evaluator to earn your certificate."></flipcard>

lessons.title: Plan Your AI Capstone
lessons.content_md:
# Plan Your AI Capstone 🗺️

A great capstone is **small, finished and well explained** — not huge and half-built. Spend an hour planning before you write code.

## Pick a Project You Can Finish in a Week

| Idea | What it shows |
|------|---------------|
| **Smart study assistant** (LLM API + a system prompt + chat history) | Prompting, API use, secure keys |
| **Document Q&A** (chunk PDFs, embed them, retrieve, answer with citations) | RAG, embeddings, grounding |
| **Image classifier** (fine-tune a pre-trained CNN on your own photos) | Transfer learning, evaluation |
| **Review sentiment API** (train a model, serve it with FastAPI) | NLP, MLOps |

## Write a One-Paragraph Brief

> **Problem:** Students waste time searching long PDFs for answers.
> **Users:** First-year college students.
> **Solution:** A CLI that answers questions about a PDF and cites the page.
> **Success looks like:** Correct, cited answers for 8 of my 10 test questions.

<flipcard front="🎯 Why define 'success' before building?" back="A measurable goal (like 8/10 correct test questions) tells you when you're done and gives the AI reviewer something concrete to check your results against."></flipcard>

## Start With a Baseline

Before anything clever, build the **simplest version that works end to end** — a keyword search, a plain prompt, or a logistic regression. Then improve and **measure** the improvement against it.

## Plan Your Repository

```text
my-ai-capstone/
├── README.md            # problem, how to run, results
├── requirements.txt     # pinned dependencies
├── .env.example         # names of required secrets (no real values!)
├── .gitignore           # .env, venv/, large data files
├── src/
│   ├── main.py          # entry point
│   └── ...
├── tests/
│   └── test_main.py     # a few small tests
└── eval/
    └── questions.csv    # your test set + expected answers
```

## Milestones

1. **Day 1–2:** Baseline running end to end.
2. **Day 3–4:** Core feature working on your test set.
3. **Day 5:** Measure results and fix the worst failures.
4. **Day 6:** README, cleanup, tests.
5. **Day 7:** Submit!

lessons.title: Ship It: Submission Checklist
lessons.content_md:
# Ship It: Submission Checklist 🚀

The **AI Capstone Evaluator** below reads your public GitHub repository — your code, README and config files — and grades it out of 100. **60 or more passes** and completes the track: you earn **+500 XP** and a shareable **certificate**. 🎓

## What the Reviewer Looks For

| Area | What earns points |
|------|-------------------|
| **It works** | A clear entry point, the core feature implemented, sensible error handling |
| **AI concepts** | The right technique for the problem, applied the way this track taught it |
| **Evaluation** | You measured results — a test set, metrics, or example outputs |
| **Code quality** | Readable names, small functions, no dead code |
| **Documentation** | A README someone else could follow |
| **Security** | No API keys or passwords in the code |

## README Template

```markdown
# Study Buddy — PDF Q&A with citations

## Problem
Students waste time searching long PDFs for answers.

## How it works
1. Splits the PDF into chunks and embeds them.
2. Retrieves the 4 most relevant chunks for each question.
3. Asks the LLM to answer only from those chunks, citing page numbers.

## Run it
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env   # add your GEMINI_API_KEY
python src/main.py notes.pdf

## Results
8/10 test questions answered correctly with valid citations (see eval/).

## What I'd improve next
Better chunking for tables; caching embeddings.
```

## Final Checklist ✅

- [ ] Repository is **public** on GitHub
- [ ] `README.md` explains the problem, how to run it and your results
- [ ] `requirements.txt` lists every dependency
- [ ] **No secrets committed** — `.env` is in `.gitignore`; only `.env.example` is pushed
- [ ] Large datasets are **not** committed — include a small sample or a download script
- [ ] Code runs from a fresh clone by following your README

<flipcard front="🔑 You accidentally committed an API key. What now?" back="Revoke (delete) the key in the provider's console immediately and create a new one. Deleting the file in a later commit is not enough — the key is still in your git history."></flipcard>

## Submit 👇

Paste your repository URL into the evaluator below. Didn't pass? Read the feedback, improve your repo and submit again — your best attempt counts.
